draft.title: Verbal and non-verbal communication
card: communication that uses words, spoken or written. The same message can be worded differently in different languages and cultures.
communication without words. It includes gestures, eye contact, personal space, facial expressions and tone of voice.
Both kinds differ between cultures. In some cultures, looking someone in the eye shows respect. In others, looking away shows respect.
A gesture or distance that feels normal in one culture can confuse or upset a person from another. The people involved may not notice that the cause is a cultural difference.
draft.remember: Words and non-verbal signals both carry meaning, and that meaning can change from one culture to another.

a.q: Which of these is an example of non-verbal communication?
opts: Standing close to someone while you talk to them
Writing a letter to a friend overseas
Explaining a rule aloud to a new student
Reading a speech to a school assembly
a.why: Personal space is communicated without words, so it is non-verbal. The other three all use words, spoken or written, so they are verbal.
a.clue: Which one sends a message without using any words?

b.q: Tom, a student from Perth, is on exchange in a country where looking a teacher in the eye is seen as rude. Tom looks at his teacher while she speaks. What is the most likely result?
opts: She may see him as disrespectful, though he meant respect
She will understand that he is paying close attention
She will see his eye contact as a spoken message
She will find his behaviour the same as in Perth
b.why: Eye contact is non-verbal, and its meaning differs between cultures. Tom means to show respect, but his teacher may read it as rude. His intention does not decide how it is understood.
b.clue: Think about what the teacher's culture says eye contact means.

a.best: Standing close to someone while you talk to them

b.best: She may see him as disrespectful, though he meant respect

problems.detail: The right option stands out. It is clearly the longest, and it is the only one with a qualifier ('may') and an extra detail ('though he meant respect'). The other three all say 'will', so a student could pick the answer without knowing the idea.
